paras: The Hurlock election riot was an exchange of gunfire between Black and white men in Hurlock, Dorchester County, Maryland, on the night of November 3, 1903, the state's election day. Three or four white men and at least one Black man were wounded, and a sheriff's party with a posse arrested fourteen Black men and took them to the jail at Cambridge. Black men were afterward indicted for rioting, and in December John Brown and six others were acquitted on the court's instruction.

Hurlock was a railroad junction town of 500 inhabitants, according to a Cambridge dispatch. That dispatch traced the trouble to a crap game the previous Saturday night, in which the Black boys were said to have won all the money and the whites "resented it by trying to 'clean them up.'" A separate Cambridge report in the New York Sun said only that trouble between the races at Hurlock "had been brewing for some time."

The fighting came on election day, Tuesday, November 3. According to the New York Sun's correspondent, Black men from around Hurlock entered the town that afternoon, "saying that they intended to take the place," and after dark shot out the street and window lights and fired on white residents. The wire dispatch placed the first shots at 11 o'clock at night, also said the Black men fired first, and added that "the fire was returned."

The wire counted three white men and one Black man wounded. The Sun instead named four wounded young white men, Samuel Parvin Young, a son of James Bennett, a Mr. Medford, and a son of the Rev. MacFarland, and said their injuries were not serious. No wounded Black man was named, but the Sun reported that several of the Black prisoners had "shots in their bodies."

Townspeople telephoned Sheriff John W. Mills at Cambridge, who set out with Deputy Sheriff Gore, W. J. Watkins and Richard Hughlett and was joined by a posse from East New Market. The officers arrested fourteen Black men, some of whom the Sun called "tough characters," and lodged them in the Cambridge jail on the morning of November 4.

In mid-November the grand jury at Cambridge indicted a number of Black men under one bill on charges of rioting on election day at Hurlock, according to a Cambridge item dated November 16. On December 5 the court instructed the jury to return verdicts of not guilty for John Brown and six other Black men indicted in connection with the riot.

The first word came in Baltimore election dispatches saying the voting had passed off peaceably except at Hurlock, where "a dispute between whites and blacks" had reportedly left twelve men wounded, a figure that could not be verified. The Montgomery Advertiser printed that bulletin on November 4, and Mississippi's Weekly Corinthian later called it a race riot "as the result of the election."

The fuller Cambridge wire story of November 4 dropped the election and blamed a crap game. The Washington Times headlined it "Three Men Wounded in Maryland Riot" and "Whites and Negroes Battle at Hurlock Over a Game of Craps," the Alexandria Gazette ran it as "Race Riot Over a Crap Game," and Delaware's Evening Journal used "Four Men Shot in Race Riot at Hurlock, Md." The Sun's "Race Clash in Maryland" described the Black men as having come to "take the place," named the white wounded and their families, and left the Black wounded anonymous.

In the Black press, the Richmond Planet carried only the Baltimore election bulletin, without comment, in its election roundup of November 7. The Baltimore Afro-American reported the indictments on November 21 in a brief headed, as printed, "Colored Men Instituted [Indicted]," set inside a column of Winchester, Virginia, news. No Black-press account of the shooting itself, editorial comment, or notice of the acquittals appears in the coverage.

Accounts differed on the cause: a crap-game quarrel (the wire), a deliberate entry into the town by Black men (the Sun), or the election (the first bulletins). Counts of the wounded ranged from twelve in the unverified bulletin to four in the Cambridge dispatches. Both detailed dispatches say the Black men fired first, but neither quotes a Black participant.

bases: The papers describe an exchange of gunfire between Black and white men in the town on election night, after which officers and a posse arrested fourteen Black men who were later indicted for rioting and acquitted on the court's instruction; no white mob attack on a Black person or community is described (A1, A5, A8, A9).

Two differently worded Cambridge dispatches agree on the shooting at Hurlock on the night of Nov. 3, the wounded, the sheriff's party and posse, and fourteen Black men jailed (A1, A5), and later reports confirm indictments and acquittals (A8, A9).

accounts.label: Court record as reported

framing.detail: Headlines 'Three Men Wounded in Maryland Riot', 'Race Riot Over a Crap Game', 'Four Men Shot in Race Riot'; the text calls it a 'race war' and says the Black men began firing.
The Sun's 'Race Clash in Maryland' presents the Black men as invaders intending to 'take the place', calls some prisoners 'tough characters', names the white wounded only.
Election-returns stories mention only an unverified 'dispute between whites and blacks' with twelve wounded.
The Richmond Planet carried the election bulletin without comment.
The Afro-American ran a brief notice of the indictments headed 'Colored Men Instituted [Indicted]' inside a Winchester news column.
